why: Let me be clear about the business first, because parts of it are extraordinary. Revenue grew 92% in a year. Starlink doubled its customers to {subs} million and now throws off {segOp.connectivity|usd} of operating profit every quarter. They have {netCashPos|usd} in the bank. Nobody else on earth can put things in orbit at this cost. None of that is in question.

The question is what you are paying, and what you are paying for. The market value is {mcap|usd} against {rev|usd} of quarterly revenue. Annualise the quarter and you are paying {psAnnualised|x0} what the company sells in a year, for a business that lost money in that quarter.

And the spending is on a different scale to the business. They spent {capexQ2|usd} on equipment in three months while selling {rev|usd}. Almost all of it went into AI computers. Over six months they took in {cfoH1|usd} of cash from operations and spent {capexH1|usd}, so the cash went backwards by roughly {fcfH1abs|usd}. That is being paid for out of the IPO and the bond, not out of the business.

Then there is who you are investing alongside. One person holds 82.4% of the votes. {relPartyDebt|usd} of the debt is owed to a fund run by a man who sits on the board. And the company has told the exchange it will skip several governance rules it would otherwise have to follow.

So: not yet. This is a company I want to own and a price I do not. Put it on the list, write down what you would pay, and note the calendar — there is a queue of newly sellable shares between now and December.

notes.title: Space Exploration Technologies — SpaceX — went public on the twelfth of June. It is now worth about one and three quarter trillion dollars, and today it moved almost sixteen percent. This is the first proper look inside the accounts, because this is the first quarter they have ever had to file. TARGET 20s.
notes.tape: Here is the whole life of this stock. All thirty-nine trading days of it. It opened at a hundred and fifty, ran to two hundred and eleven in three days, then fell almost half. That low was the fifth of August — the day after the first earnings report. And then it turned around hard. TARGET 22s.
notes.findings: Four things in here that I have not seen anyone else talk about. Every one of them comes out of documents filed in the last eight weeks. We will do each one properly. TARGET 26s.
notes.business: Three businesses under one roof. Space puts things in orbit. Connectivity is Starlink. AI is Grok and the data centres. Hold on to the fact that they are wildly different in size and in health. TARGET 22s.
notes.segments: Here is the shape of it. Connectivity makes all the money. Space loses money. AI loses more. The company as a whole lost a hundred and forty-three million in the quarter. TARGET 26s.
notes.starlink: This is the good news, and it is genuinely good. Twelve million subscribers, double a year ago. One point seven billion dollars of operating profit in a quarter. If this were a standalone company it would be one of the best businesses in the world. TARGET 24s.
notes.arpu: But look underneath it. Revenue per customer has gone from eighty-five dollars a month to sixty-six. That is a twenty-two percent fall. The release says ARPU was maintained — and against last quarter it was. Against last year it fell hard. Doubling your customers while cutting your price by a fifth is growth, but it is a different kind of growth than the headline suggests. TARGET 30s.
notes.space: And the rocket company launched less. Thirty-eight launches against forty-six. Mass to orbit down twenty-six percent. Revenue went up because the mix shifted to paying customers, but the machine did less work. TARGET 26s.
notes.capex: Now the number that matters most. Eighteen point four billion dollars of equipment bought in three months, against seven point eight billion of sales. Almost all of it is AI computers. TARGET 28s.
notes.cash: Over six months the business brought in three and a half billion of cash and spent twenty-eight and a half billion on equipment. That is twenty-five billion out the door, funded by the IPO and the bond, not by the business. TARGET 28s.
notes.balance: On the balance sheet, this is now more of a computer company than a rocket company. Thirty-five billion dollars of servers against fourteen billion of satellites. TARGET 22s.
notes.ebitda: Watch this one carefully, because it is the most common trick in AI accounting. The AI division reported positive adjusted earnings of one point one billion. It lost one point three billion. The difference is that they added back the depreciation on the computers they had just bought. TARGET 30s.
notes.related: This is the one nobody is talking about. Thirteen point three billion dollars of the debt is owed to Valor Equity Partners. The man who runs Valor sits on SpaceX's board. And the accountants ruled the deal a failed sale-leaseback, which is why it shows up as borrowing. Six months ago it was four and a half billion. TARGET 32s.
notes.related13g: And then this landed this morning. A Schedule thirteen-G, filed today, dated back to June thirtieth. Antonio Gracias — the same director whose fund is owed the thirteen point three billion — beneficially owns five hundred and three million shares. Six and a half percent of the Class A stock. Here is the part I want you to sit with: it is held across thirty separate entities, and the filing says in writing that not one of them reaches five percent on its own. Five percent is the line where you have to tell the public. So he is the biggest lender and a six and a half percent owner at the same time, and until this morning there was no way to see the second half. Nothing here is illegal. But you are buying into a company where the same man gets paid interest as the lender and gains as an owner. TARGET 34s.
notes.concentration: Two customers are nearly thirty-eight percent of all revenue. One of them was not even a ten percent customer a year ago. TARGET 22s.
notes.commitments: They have signed up to spend twenty-eight billion dollars they cannot cancel, and twenty-two billion of that falls in a single year — twenty twenty-seven. TARGET 24s.
notes.lockup: Here is the calendar nobody put in a headline. The lockup does not end all at once. Twenty percent came free on the sixth of August. There was a bonus ten percent available if the stock had held thirty percent above the IPO price — it did not, zero days out of ten. Then seven percent more on each of five dates between now and October, twenty-eight percent after the next results, and everything on the eighth of December. TARGET 34s.
notes.governance: One person holds eighty-two point four percent of the votes, through shares that carry ten votes each. The company is officially a controlled company, which lets it skip several Nasdaq governance rules. TARGET 24s.
notes.dilution: And there are one point three billion shares promised to the founder that do not appear in the share count yet, because the targets have not been hit. One tranche of them only vests if SpaceX builds data centres in space. TARGET 26s.
notes.valuation: So what are you paying. Annualise this quarter and it is about fifty-six times sales, for a company that lost money. There is no guidance to check that against, because SpaceX gives none. TARGET 26s.
notes.peers: Against the most expensive software companies on the market, SpaceX is in a category of its own — and those companies make profits. TARGET 24s.
notes.street: Nine to ten analysts cover it and they cannot agree at all. For twenty twenty-seven the estimates run from a loss to three dollars forty-six a share. TARGET 22s.
notes.verdict: Six dimensions. The business scores brilliantly. The price and the governance do not. TARGET 24s.
notes.twolists: What is working, and what I would watch. TARGET 20s.
notes.fairvalue: Here is my own arithmetic, and I want you to see how generous it has to be. TARGET 24s.
notes.call: Not yet. Not because it is a bad company — because it is a wonderful company at a price that already assumes the hard part works. Let's go to the chart. TARGET 30s.
